unit.unitOverview: Research is finding out about something in a careful, organised way, from more than one source, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a search engine. Real research means asking a good question, gathering information from several sources, checking whether you can trust them, recording the important parts in your own words, and saying where everything came from.

explainers.title: Welcome to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This subject is different from most others you have studied. It is not about memorising a long list of facts. Instead, it teaches you a set of thinking skills that you can use for the rest of your life, in any subject and in the real world around you.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you will grow all of them over your years here:

This unit is all about the very first skill: Research. Everything you build here will support the other five skills later, because you cannot analyse, evaluate or communicate an idea well until you have researched it properly.

You may be wondering why these skills matter beyond school. Think about the choices adults make every day. A parent comparing two clinics for a sick child, a shopkeeper deciding which goods will sell, a community leader choosing where to dig a new well: all of them are really doing research. They ask questions, gather information, judge who to trust, and decide. The learner who practises these skills now will make better decisions for their whole life. That is why we begin here.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in Ehel Academy's self-paced way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss as a class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a real conversation. Say your ideas out loud or type them, and let the tutor push your thinking further.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, available 24 hours a day. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a study partner and a whole class of classmates in one. It will discuss your ideas, ask you questions, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work, ask the questions that matter most, and get to know the other learners.

explainers.title: Meet Amal, our researcher for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 7 learner all the way through the unit. Her name is Amal, and she is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

During the long dry season, Amal notices that her neighbours spend a lot of time collecting water. Some families walk a long way to the nearest water point, and the queues can be very long in the morning. Amal starts to wonder: do all the families in her neighbourhood have enough safe water, and what would help the most?

That question becomes Amal's research project for this unit. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Amal does with it. By the end, she will have real findings she can share. You will be doing the very same thing with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a global topic that also matters right where you live. You will keep returning to it, lesson after lesson, and each new skill adds another piece to it.

Here are some global topics that are also very real in the Horn of Africa. Any of these could become your Challenge:

You do not have to choose right now. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any topic that makes you curious or a little bit annoyed. Strong curiosity and 'someone should fix this' feelings are excellent signs of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: Clean water for every family
Education for all, including girls staying in school
Plastic waste in our streets and on our coasts
Renewable energy, such as solar power
Healthy food and good school meals
Road safety on busy streets
Protecting endangered wildlife, such as sea turtles on the Berbera coast
Why people move from the countryside to cities (migration)

explainers.title: What is research, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think 'research' just means typing a question into a search engine and reading the first answer. Real research is more careful than that. Research is finding out about something in an organised way, from more than one source, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to others.

Good research usually moves through a cycle:

You will learn every step in this unit. Notice that 'search the internet' is only a small part of one step. Researchers also talk to people, watch what happens, and read printed material.
bullets: Ask a clear question worth answering.
Decide where the information could come from.
Gather information from several sources.
Check whether each source can be trusted.
Record the important parts in your own words.
Organise and summarise what you found.
Say where your information came from (reference it).

explainers.title: Keep a research journal
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a simple habit that real researchers use: keep a research journal. This can be a notebook or a document where you record everything about your Challenge as you go. Each time you work, write the date and jot down what you did, what you found, and what you want to do next.

A research journal matters for three reasons. It keeps your sources and notes in one place so nothing gets lost. It shows how your thinking changes over time, which you will need later for Reflection. And it makes writing up your findings far easier, because the work is already there. Keep your journal beside you as you read the rest of this file.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Asking good research questions
explainers.body:
Every strong research project starts with a strong question. A weak question wastes your time, because you can never really answer it. A good research question has three features. It is clear, it is focused, and it can be argued.

Watch out for three common problems. A question can be too broad, too narrow, or too vague. Here is how to spot each one:

The good news is that most weak questions can be rescued. You keep the topic you care about, then make the question clearer, narrow it to a place or a group, and remove any hidden opinion. A question you can fix is not a failure; it is a normal step on the way to a strong one.
bullets: Clear means someone else can read your question and know exactly what you are asking.
Focused means the question is not too broad and not too narrow. Too broad and you cannot find one answer; too narrow and there is not enough to find out.
Can be argued means people could reasonably give different answers, so you have to weigh evidence and form an opinion, rather than looking up one simple fact.
Too broad: 'What is poverty?' You could study this for years and never finish. Narrow it to a place and a group of people.
Too narrow: 'How many taps are in my school?' You can answer this in one minute by counting, so there is nothing to research or argue.
Too vague: 'Why are phones bad?' This is unclear and it hides an opinion. It assumes phones are bad before you have any evidence.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Breaking your big question into sub-questions
explainers.body: A good research question is often too big to answer in one go. The trick is to break it into smaller sub-questions. Each sub-question is easier to research, and together they help you answer the big one.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Knowing your sources (primary and secondary)
explainers.body:
Information comes from sources. A source is anywhere your information comes from: a book, a website, a video, a person, or something you see with your own eyes. Sources come in two main types.

Strong research usually uses both. Secondary sources give you the bigger picture and facts that others have already found. Primary sources let you find out what is true right here, in your own community, which no book could tell you.
bullets: Primary sources give you first-hand information that you gather yourself. Interviews you carry out, surveys you run, and things you observe are all primary sources.
Secondary sources are made by someone else who studied the topic before you. Books, news articles, websites and reports are secondary sources.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Choosing a research method to test a prediction
explainers.body:
Before gathering primary information, good researchers often make a prediction. A prediction is a smart guess about what you will find. Then you choose a method to test whether your prediction is right. The three most common methods for Year 7 are:

You choose the method that fits your question. If you want numbers from many people, use a survey. If you want the full story from one person, use an interview. If you want to know what really happens, use observation.
bullets: Survey or questionnaire — the same set of questions given to many people, to find out what a lot of people think or do.
Interview — a deeper conversation with one person or a small group, to understand their views in detail.
Observation — carefully watching and recording what actually happens.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Judging whether a source can be trusted
explainers.body: Not everything you read or watch is true. Before you use a source, ask yourself four quick questions: Who wrote it? When was it made? Can I trust it? Is it relevant to my question?
bullets: Who wrote or made it, and do they really know about the topic?
When was it made? Old information may be out of date.
Can I trust it? Does it give evidence, or is it just an opinion? Do other good sources agree?
Is it relevant? Does it actually help answer my question, or is it just interesting?

explainers.title: Skill 6: Finding the information you need
explainers.body: When you use a search engine well, you save time and find better information. Weak searching means typing a whole sentence and clicking the first link. Strong searching follows clear steps.
bullets: Decide exactly what information you need before you start.
Choose three to six important keywords, not a full sentence.
Look past the first few results; good sources are often further down.
Skim-read a page quickly. Is it clear? Is it useful? If yes, save or note it.
Check who made the page and when, using Skill 5.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Taking notes in your own words
explainers.body:
Once you find a good source, you do not copy it. You take notes. Notes are short reminders of the important ideas, written in your own words. Writing in your own words proves you understood the idea, and it keeps you from copying.

Two things help you take strong notes:
bullets: Find the main idea of each paragraph. A useful trick is to look for words that are repeated, because writers repeat the words that matter most.
Notice the subject-specific words — the special words linked to the topic, such as borehole, drought, or filter for a water topic. Write these down, because you will need them.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Recording and organising your findings
explainers.body: After you gather information, especially from a survey, you need to record and organise it so that a pattern becomes clear. A pile of answers means nothing until you sort it. Tables, tally charts and simple bar charts are perfect for this.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Summarising what you found
explainers.body:
A summary is a short version of a longer text or of your findings, written in your own words, that keeps only the most important ideas. A good summary is much shorter than the original and never just copies it. These sentence starters help:

When you summarise, ask yourself three checking questions: Is it the right length? Does it keep the key information? Is it in my own words rather than copied? If you can answer yes to all three, you have a strong summary.
bullets: The text is about ...
The main idea is ...
In the first part, we find out ...
Next, we learn ...
Finally, it tells us ...

explainers.title: Skill 10: Referencing your sources, and never copying
explainers.body:
When you use someone else's work, you must give them credit by writing a reference. A reference is a note that says exactly where your information came from. A reference list is all your references gathered at the end of your work.

Referencing matters for two reasons. First, it is honest: taking someone's words or ideas and pretending they are yours is called plagiarism, and it is a kind of copying we never do. Second, it is useful: a reader can check your sources and trust your work more.

explainers.title: Staying safe and fair when you research
explainers.body:
Because research means going out into the world and online, a good researcher also learns to stay safe and to be fair. These habits are part of the skill, not extra rules.

Staying safe online. When you search and read online, protect yourself:

Being fair to different viewpoints. Global Perspectives is about seeing an issue from many sides. On almost any topic, people hold different views, and a fair researcher listens to all of them evenly before deciding. Look at an issue from four levels: how it affects you personally, your local community, your nation, and the wider global world. A topic like clean water looks different at each level, and seeing all four makes your research much richer.
bullets: Never share your full name, home address, school details or photos with strangers online.
If a page asks you to sign up, download something, or 'click to win', stop and check with a trusted adult.
If a source upsets or worries you, close it and talk to your teacher or family.

explainers.title: How research feeds the other five skills
explainers.body:
Research is the first Global Perspectives skill for a reason: it feeds all the others. Once you have researched a topic well, the rest becomes possible.

So the effort you put into research now is never wasted. It is the foundation the whole subject is built on.
bullets: Analysis needs good information before you can break a topic into causes and effects.
Evaluation needs trustworthy sources before you can judge how strong an argument is.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your research changed your mind.
Collaboration works better when everyone brings well-researched ideas to share.
Communication is only as strong as the research behind it; facts make your message believable.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the research cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every research skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one smooth cycle you can use for any topic:
bullets: Ask a clear, focused, arguable question, and break it into sub-questions.
Decide which sources and methods fit, and make a prediction to test.
Gather information from primary and secondary sources.
Judge whether each source can be trusted.
Take notes in your own words and organise your findings.
Summarise what you learned.
Reference every source you used.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Analysis. Once you can research a topic well, analysis teaches you to break it apart and ask why things happen and what the consequences are. Strong research now will make strong analysis much easier later. Well done for starting your Global Perspectives journey with a solid foundation.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle, and the skill is the destination.
We will use real-world topics such as clean water, plastic waste and road safety, but the point is not to become an expert on water.
The point is to become a strong researcher who could find out about almost anything.

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: A good researcher weighs many viewpoints fairly instead of only their own.
For example, a question such as: Should our school calendar include holidays for both Eid and Christmas? forces you to listen to different families evenly.
Seeing an issue from many sides, without promoting one side, is at the heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: Quick clues from a website address
lines: An address ending in .gov (often with a country code) is usually an official government site and is often reliable.
An address ending in .org is often a non-profit organisation and can be a good source.
If the address contains the word wiki, or the page is social media, take care: many people can edit it, so the information may not be correct.
These are only clues, not proof. Always check who wrote it and whether other sources agree.

bigIdeas.title: How to write a good note
lines: Keep notes short: a few words, not full sentences.
Use bullet points.
Use your own words, never copy word for word.
Write down the source next to your notes, so you can reference it later.

bigIdeas.title: The five parts of a reference
lines: 1. The author (who wrote it).
2. The title (what it is called).
3. The date it was published.
4. Where to find it (for example, the website address).
5. The date you looked at it.

bigIdeas.title: Watch out for bias
lines: Bias is when a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
A source is not automatically wrong because it has a viewpoint, but you should notice the viewpoint.
Balance a strong opinion from one side by finding a good source from another side.
Being fair does not mean having no opinion; it means forming your opinion only after hearing many sides.

bigIdeas.title: Quick clues from a web address
lines: Ends in .gov (often with a country code): usually an official government site, often reliable.
Ends in .org: often a non-profit organisation, often a good source.
Contains wiki, or is social media: anyone may have edited it, so take care and check elsewhere.
Clues are not proof. Always check who wrote it and whether other sources agree.

bigIdeas.title: Reference format and example
lines: Format: Author (Year). Title. [Online] Available at: web address (Accessed date).
Example: Farah (2023). Water Points in Hargeisa. [Online] Available at: www.example.org/water-hargeisa (Accessed 12/03/2024).
This example shows the format only; it is not a real source.
Sentence starters you can use when you write about a source:

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one global topic that also matters where you live. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely care about.
By the end you will have real research you can share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: A hint before you check with your tutor
lines: One of these hides an opinion and pushes you to one answer.
One is a simple fact you could answer in five seconds.
One is so broad you could write a whole book and still not finish.
One can genuinely be argued with evidence on both sides.

bigIdeas.title: The jumbled details
lines: Title: Solar Power for Homes
Date you looked at it: 05/04/2024
Author: Bello
Web address: www.example.org/solar-homes
Year published: 2022

Use this pattern to build it: Author (Year). Title. [Online] Available at: web address (Accessed date). Write out your finished reference, then write a reference for one real source you found in Activity 6.

bigIdeas.title: Source passage: Plastic bags in our markets
lines: Many bags end up in the street, where wind blows them into drains. When the rains come, blocked drains cannot carry the water away, and streets can flood.
Some bags reach the coast, where sea animals such as turtles can mistake them for food. Reusable cloth bags, used again and again, would cut this waste sharply.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a good survey question
lines: It is clear about what it is asking.
It relates to your topic and purpose.
It can be answered fairly quickly.
It is not leading. A leading question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Do you agree that our water is terrible?
Check each of your questions against that list. Rewrite any question that is unclear or leading. For example, change 'Do you agree the water is bad?' into 'How would you describe the water you use?'.

models.title: Research happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine you want to buy the best value schoolbag in the market.
You ask a clear question: which bag lasts longest for the lowest price?
You gather information: you feel the cloth, ask the seller, and ask two friends who own bags.
You judge your sources: the seller wants a sale, so you trust your friends a little more.
You decide, using what you found. That is real research, and you already do it.

So research is not a strange school-only activity. It is a careful, honest way of finding things out that you can get better and better at. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, with more skill, and about topics that matter to your community.

models.title: Amal's example: sharpening the question
lines: Amal's first idea was: Why is water bad? That is vague and it hides an opinion.
Her second idea was: What is water? That is far too broad.
Her strong final question is: How can families in my neighbourhood get safe water more easily in the dry season?
It is clear, it is focused on her neighbourhood and the dry season, and it can be argued, because different solutions are possible.

models.title: Amal's example: her sub-questions
lines: Big question: How can families in my neighbourhood get safe water more easily in the dry season?
Sub-question 1: Where do families get their water now?
Sub-question 2: How far do they have to walk, and how long do they queue?
Sub-question 3: Is the water safe to drink?
Sub-question 4: What change would help families the most?

Notice that each sub-question could be researched on its own. Sub-question 2 might be answered with a survey, while sub-question 3 might need information from a health organisation. Sub-questions turn one huge task into a set of smaller, doable ones.

models.title: Karim's example: sub-questions for plastic waste
lines: Big question: How could my town cut down on plastic waste from the market?
Sub-question 1: How much plastic does the market use in a day?
Sub-question 2: Where does the waste go, and what harm does it cause?
Sub-question 3: What are people already doing to reduce it?
Sub-question 4: Would reusable bags work here, and would people accept them?

A good set of sub-questions covers the topic from several angles: what is happening now, why it matters, and what could change. If all your sub-questions ask almost the same thing, spread them out to cover more of the topic.

models.title: Leila's example: road safety in Mogadishu
lines: Leila wants to know why a road near her school in Mogadishu feels dangerous.
Secondary sources: a news report about traffic, and a road-safety charity's web page.
Primary sources: standing safely near the road to watch how drivers behave, and interviewing a shopkeeper who sees the road all day.
Together, the two types give Leila a much fuller answer than either could alone.

Sources can also be print or multimedia. Print sources are on paper: books, newspapers and printed reports. Multimedia sources are digital: websites, videos, audio recordings and images. Each has strengths. A printed report may be checked carefully before it is published; a short video may explain an idea quickly and clearly. A good researcher is comfortable using a range of both, and does not rely on only one kind.

models.title: Yasmin's example: education for girls
lines: Yasmin wants to know why some girls in her area leave school early.
Secondary sources: a report from an education charity, and a printed newspaper article.
Primary source: a respectful interview with an older student who left and later returned.
The report gives the big picture, but the interview gives a real story the report could never capture.

models.title: Amal's example: making and testing a prediction
lines: Amal's prediction: I think most families in my neighbourhood walk more than 20 minutes to collect water in the dry season.
Best method: a short survey given to many neighbours, because she wants numbers from a lot of people.
If she only wanted one family's full story, an interview would fit better.

models.title: Omar's example: a different method for a different question
lines: Omar predicts that solar lamps would help students study after dark.
He chooses interviews with a few families who already own solar lamps, because he wants their detailed experience, not just a yes or no.

Often the strongest research uses more than one method. You might run a survey to get numbers from many people, then interview one or two of them to understand the numbers in more depth. A survey can tell you that many families walk far for water; an interview can tell you how that feels and why it is hard. Numbers and stories together are more convincing than either alone.
Whatever method you choose, plan it kindly and safely. Ask people politely, let them say no, and never share anyone's name without asking. Good researchers respect the people who help them.

models.title: Idris's example: sea turtles on the Berbera coast
lines: Idris finds two pages about endangered sea turtles near Berbera.
One is on a wildlife organisation's .org site, written by named scientists, updated last year.
The other is an unsigned social-media post with no date and no evidence.
Idris trusts the first far more, and looks for a second good source to confirm it.

models.title: Nadia's example: healthy school meals
lines: Nadia's question is about healthy school meals for students her age.
Weak search: Why is school food not very healthy and what can we do about it.
Strong search keywords: healthy school meals children nutrition.
She then looks for a health organisation's page rather than the very first result.
Choosing sharp keywords is a skill in itself. Pull out the two or three most important ideas in your question and search for those, then add or change one word at a time if you need to.

models.title: Karim's example: notes on plastic waste
lines: Karim reads a paragraph that repeats the words plastic bags, market and drains.
His note reads: Plastic bags from the market block drains and cause flooding.
That is shorter than the paragraph, in his own words, and captures the main idea.

models.title: Amal's example: organising her survey
lines: Amal asked 20 neighbours how long they walk to collect water in the dry season.
She sorted the answers into three groups: under 10 minutes, 10 to 20 minutes, and more than 20 minutes.
A simple table showed that 12 of the 20 families walk more than 20 minutes.
That result supported her prediction, and it was easy to see once it was organised.

How you present your findings depends on your audience and on the kind of information you gathered. Numbers often suit a chart; personal stories from an interview often suit a few careful quotations. Always pick the form that makes your finding easiest to understand.

models.title: Karim's example: a one-line summary
lines: Karim's summary of his plastic-waste source: The text is about plastic bags in local markets. The main idea is that plastic bags block drains and harm animals, and that reusable bags would help.
It is short, in his own words, and keeps the key point.

models.title: What a finished reference looks like
lines: Farah (2023). Water Points in Hargeisa. [Online] Available at: www.example.org/water-hargeisa (Accessed 12/03/2024).
This is an illustration of the format only. Notice all five parts are there.
You will practise real referencing in the Activities file and find ready-made sentence starters in the Skills Toolkit.

models.title: Amal's whole journey, from worry to findings
lines: Skill 1: She turned a worry about water into a clear, arguable question.
Skill 2: She broke it into four sub-questions.
Skills 3 and 4: She chose secondary reports and a primary survey, and made a prediction to test.
Skill 5: She checked that her sources could be trusted.
Skills 6 and 7: She searched well and took notes in her own words.
Skill 8: She organised her survey into a table and found that 12 of 20 families walk more than 20 minutes.
Skills 9 and 10: She summarised her findings and referenced every source.

By following this cycle, Amal turned an everyday worry about water into real, organised findings she can share with her teacher and her community. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge topic, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model mind map: plastic waste
lines: In the middle: plastic waste in my town.
Branches: How much plastic does one family throw away each week? Where does it end up? Who is affected most? What could replace plastic bags? Do people want to change? What do market sellers think?
Notice that these questions come from different angles, which is exactly what you want.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic: clean water in my neighbourhood.
Research question: How can families in my neighbourhood get safe water more easily in the dry season?
Sub-questions: Where do families get water now? How far do they walk? Is the water safe? What would help most?

models.title: Copying versus your own words
lines: Imagine a sentence: Many bags end up in the street, where wind blows them into drains.
A copied note just repeats those exact words, which is not allowed.
A good note in your own words might be: wind carries loose bags into drains.
Same meaning, your words, much shorter. That is the goal.

models.title: A model: Amal presenting her survey
lines: Finding: 12 of the 20 families she asked walk more than 20 minutes for water.
Best form: a simple bar chart, because the information is numbers and a chart shows the pattern at a glance.
Audience: her teacher and community, who can see the problem quickly from the chart.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 1 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Research.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, why is research a useful skill even outside of school?
Then tell the tutor which of the six skills you think will be easiest for you, and which will be hardest, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think research means.
Ask the tutor: Is my definition missing anything important?
Then ask it to give you one everyday example of research that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Write three possible research questions about a topic you like.
Tell all three to your AI tutor and ask: Which is the strongest, and why?
Ask the tutor to help you reword your weakest question so it becomes clear, focused, and arguable.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your big research question.
Ask it to help you break the question into three or four sub-questions.
Then check together: does answering all the sub-questions really add up to answering the big one?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic.
Ask it to help you list two secondary sources and two primary sources you could use.
Then ask: Which one primary source would teach me something no book could?

toolkit.title: The research cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your topic, good research follows the same seven steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Question: ask a clear, focused, arguable question, and break it into sub-questions.
Plan: decide which sources and methods fit, and make a prediction to test.
Gather: collect information from primary and secondary sources.
Check: judge whether each source can be trusted.
Record: take notes in your own words and organise your findings.
Summarise: write the key ideas briefly, in your own words.
Reference: say exactly where every piece of information came from.

toolkit.title: The Research skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Research is finding out about something in a careful, organised way, from more than one source, so that you can trust what you learn and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a search engine. Real research means asking a good question, gathering information from several sources, checking whether you can trust them, recording the important parts in your own words, and saying where everything came from.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always use more than one source, because one source can be wrong or one-sided. Second, always write in your own words and say where your information came from, because that is honest and it helps others trust your work. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 7 Research objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong research looks like at this stage. Here are the official Research objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Construct relevant research questions.
Ask clear, focused questions that are worth researching.
Identify and begin to reference a range of print and multimedia sources, and use them to locate relevant information and answer research questions.
Find useful books, websites and videos, use them to answer your question, and say where they came from.
Select an appropriate method and conduct research to test predictions and begin to answer a research question.
Choose the right method, such as a survey, interview or observation, and use it to test a prediction.
Select, organise and record relevant information from a range of sources and findings from research, using appropriate methods.
Pick out what matters, take notes in your own words, and organise your findings clearly.

toolkit.title: Primary and secondary sources
toolkit.intro: Strong research usually uses both types. Secondary sources give the bigger picture and the facts others have already found; primary sources tell you what is true in your own community, which no book could know. A good rule is to start with secondary sources to understand the topic, then use primary research to test it where you live.

rows: Primary source
First-hand information you gather yourself.
An interview, a survey you run, your own observation.
Secondary source
Information made earlier by someone else.
A book, a news article, a website, a report.

toolkit.title: Choosing a research method
toolkit.intro: Pick the method that fits what you want to find out. Make a prediction first, then use the method to test it.

rows: Survey or questionnaire
When you want numbers or opinions from many people.
How far do families walk for water?
Interview
When you want one person's detailed story or views.
What is it like to run the local water point?
Observation
When you want to know what really happens.
How do drivers behave near the school gate?

toolkit.title: Turning a question into search keywords
toolkit.intro:
Search engines work best with a few sharp keywords, not a whole sentence. To make keywords, take your question and keep only the most important words.

Then improve your search one step at a time: add a place, swap a word for a similar one, or make it more specific until the results fit your question. If you get too many results, add a word to narrow it; if you get too few, remove a word or try a simpler one.
items: Question: How can families in my neighbourhood get safe water in the dry season?
Weak search: type the whole question as a sentence.
Strong keywords: safe water families dry season.

toolkit.title: Template: Taking notes from a source
toolkit.intro: Copy this table for each source. Keep notes short, in bullet points, and in your own words.

rows: Source and reference
Main idea (one sentence)
Subject-specific words
Note from paragraph 1
Note from paragraph 2
Note from paragraph 3

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for a summary
toolkit.intro:
Use these to write a short summary in your own words:

Then check: Is it the right length? Does it keep the key information? Is it in my own words, not copied?
items: The text is about ...
The main idea is ...
In the first part, we find out ...
Next, we learn ...
Finally, it tells us ...

toolkit.title: Referencing your sources
toolkit.intro: A reference has five parts: the author, the title, the date published, where to find it, and the date you looked at it. Put all your references together in a reference list at the end of your work. The easiest way to reference well is to write the source down the moment you use it, rather than trying to remember it later.
items: According to ... (author, year), ...
One source, ... (author, year), explains that ...
As reported by ... (author, year), ...
This information comes from ... (author, year).

toolkit.title: Question starters for surveys and interviews
toolkit.intro:
Use these to write clear, fair questions. Keep them short and never leading.

Avoid starters like 'Don't you agree that ...?' or 'Isn't it obvious that ...?'. These are leading and push people toward one answer.
items: How often do you ...?
How would you describe ...?
What do you think about ...?
How far / how long / how many ...?
What would help you most with ...?
Can you tell me about a time when ...? (good for interviews)

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this a good research question?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, reword your question.
items: Clear — someone else would understand exactly what I am asking.
Focused — it is not too broad and not too narrow.
Arguable — people could give different answers, so I must weigh evidence.
Cared about — it matters to me and to other people.
Findable — I will actually be able to find information to answer it.

checklists.title: Checklist: Can I trust this source?
checklists.intro: Ask these four questions about every source before you use it.
items: Who wrote or made it, and do they really know the topic?
When was it made? Could it be out of date?
Can I trust it? Does it give evidence, and do other good sources agree?
Is it relevant? Does it actually help answer my question?

challenge.intro: Look back at the topic list in the Lesson file (clean water, education, plastic waste, renewable energy, healthy food, road safety, endangered wildlife, migration). Choose one that matters in your area, or think of your own. The best Challenge topic is one you are genuinely curious about, because you will be living with it for the whole unit. If nothing jumps out yet, that is fine; the mind-map in the next activity will help you find your spark.
topics: Write your chosen topic in one sentence: 'The topic I am working on is ...'.
Write one reason you care about it.
Write one reason you think other people in your community care about it too.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Mind-map your questions
activities.label: Activity 2: Mind-map your questions
activities.intro:
Before you can pick a research question, you need lots of questions to choose from. A mind map helps you get them all out of your head and onto the page.

Aim for quantity first. A messy mind map with many questions is far more useful than a tidy one with only two.
steps: Write your topic in the middle of a page and draw a circle around it.
Around it, write as many questions about the topic as you can, at least eight. Do not judge them yet; just get them down.
Draw lines linking any questions that seem to belong together.

boxes.title: A model mind map: plastic waste
lines: In the middle: plastic waste in my town.
Branches: How much plastic does one family throw away each week? Where does it end up? Who is affected most? What could replace plastic bags? Do people want to change? What do market sellers think?
Notice that these questions come from different angles, which is exactly what you want.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your mind-map questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Which two or three questions look the most promising, and why?
Ask the tutor to suggest one interesting question I did not think of.

activities.title: Judge weak and strong questions
activities.label: Activity 3: Judge weak and strong questions
activities.intro:
Remember the three features of a good research question: it is clear, it is focused, and it can be argued. Use them to judge the questions below. For each one, decide if it is strong or weak, and write down why.

Rank these four questions from strongest (1) to weakest (4):

As you rank them, ask yourself for each: Is it something people care about? Is it too broad, too narrow or too vague? Could I actually find information to answer it? Write a short reason for your order.
steps: A. When do children start school?
B. Should we remove all sugar from school meals?
C. What is poverty?
D. Why is plastic bad?

boxes.title: A hint before you check with your tutor
lines: One of these hides an opinion and pushes you to one answer.
One is a simple fact you could answer in five seconds.
One is so broad you could write a whole book and still not finish.
One can genuinely be argued with evidence on both sides.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your ranking, from strongest to weakest, with your reasons.
Ask it whether it agrees, and to explain any place where it would rank differently.
Then ask the tutor to help you reword the weakest question so it becomes strong.

activities.title: Write and sharpen your own research question
activities.label: Activity 4: Write and sharpen your own research question
activities.intro: Now build the research question for your Challenge. Take your time; this question will guide everything else you do in the unit. It is completely normal to write a question, decide it is weak, and rewrite it two or three times. That reworking is the skill, not a mistake.
steps: Write down what most interests you about your topic.
Write three questions about the topic.
Look at your three questions. What do they have in common?
Draft one research question that captures what you most want to find out.
Check it: is it clear, focused, and arguable? Reword it until all three are true.
Write three sub-questions that would help you answer your main question.

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Topic: clean water in my neighbourhood.
Research question: How can families in my neighbourhood get safe water more easily in the dry season?
Sub-questions: Where do families get water now? How far do they walk? Is the water safe? What would help most?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor your research question and three sub-questions.
Ask: Is my question clear, focused, and arguable? Where is it weakest?
Ask the tutor whether my sub-questions really add up to answering my main question.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your final research question and sub-questions.
Share them in your next teacher session and ask if they are a good fit for the topic.

activities.title: Sort the sources
activities.label: Activity 5: Sort the sources
activities.intro:
Before you hunt for your own sources, warm up by sorting these. For each one, decide whether it is a primary source (first-hand, gathered by you) or a secondary source (made earlier by someone else).

Write P or S next to each letter. Then write one sentence explaining the difference between the two kinds in your own words.
steps: A. A survey you give to twenty neighbours.
B. A newspaper article about traffic in Mogadishu.
C. Watching a water point for an hour and noting what happens.
D. A page on a wildlife charity's website.
E. An interview you record with a shopkeeper.
F. A printed government report on school attendance.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any that you got wrong, in a simple way.
Ask the tutor: For my Challenge topic, would primary or secondary sources be more useful, and why?

activities.title: Source hunt and referencing table
activities.label: Activity 6: Source hunt and referencing table
activities.intro:
Now find sources for your question. Aim for a mix: at least one primary idea (a person you could interview or something you could observe) and two secondary sources (such as a website, report or article). Try to include both print and multimedia.

As you find each source, record it in a referencing table like the one below. Filling it in now saves you a lot of time later, and makes your final reference list easy. Aim for quality over quantity: three sources you can really trust are worth more than ten you cannot.

Use the four trust questions from the Lesson file as you choose: Who wrote it? When? Can I trust it? Is it relevant? Reject any source you cannot trust, even if it is easy to find.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the sources you found and read out your table.
Ask it: Which of my sources looks the most trustworthy, and which looks the weakest?
Ask the tutor to help me turn one row of my table into a full, correct reference.

activities.title: Practise writing a reference
activities.label: Activity 7: Practise writing a reference
activities.intro: A reference has five parts: the author, the title, the date published, where to find it, and the date you looked at it. Practise putting them in order. Below are the jumbled details of one source. Arrange them into a correct reference.

boxes.title: The jumbled details
lines: Title: Solar Power for Homes
Date you looked at it: 05/04/2024
Author: Bello
Web address: www.example.org/solar-homes
Year published: 2022

Use this pattern to build it: Author (Year). Title. [Online] Available at: web address (Accessed date). Write out your finished reference, then write a reference for one real source you found in Activity 6.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your finished reference to your AI tutor and ask it to check the five parts are all there and in order.
Ask it to help you reference one real source from your own source hunt.
Ask the tutor: Why does it matter that I include the date I looked at a website?

activities.title: Note-taking and summarising
activities.label: Activity 8: Note-taking and summarising
activities.intro:
Read the short passage below. It is your source for this task. You will take notes in your own words, then write a summary. Remember the two tricks: to find the main idea, look for words that are repeated, and to write a good note, keep it short and in your own words.

When you finish, check your summary with the three questions: Is it the right length? Does it keep the key information? Is it in your own words, not copied?
steps: Write the main idea of the whole passage in one sentence.
Write two or three subject-specific words from the passage (words linked to the topic).
Write one short bullet-point note, in your own words, for each of the three paragraphs.
Now write a summary of the passage using the sentence starters: 'The text is about ...', 'The main idea is ...', 'Finally, it tells us ...'.

boxes.title: Source passage: Plastic bags in our markets
lines: Many bags end up in the street, where wind blows them into drains. When the rains come, blocked drains cannot carry the water away, and streets can flood.
Some bags reach the coast, where sea animals such as turtles can mistake them for food. Reusable cloth bags, used again and again, would cut this waste sharply.

boxes.title: Copying versus your own words
lines: Imagine a sentence: Many bags end up in the street, where wind blows them into drains.
A copied note just repeats those exact words, which is not allowed.
A good note in your own words might be: wind carries loose bags into drains.
Same meaning, your words, much shorter. That is the goal.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your notes and your summary to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Have I copied any phrases, or is this really in my own words?
Ask the tutor whether I found the true main idea, and how to make my summary clearer.

activities.title: Plan a small survey or interview
activities.label: Activity 9: Plan a small survey or interview
activities.intro: Time to plan some primary research: information you gather yourself, first-hand. This is often the most exciting part, because you find out something no book could tell you about your own community. First make a prediction, then choose a method to test it, then write your questions.
steps: Write a prediction about your topic, starting with 'I think ...'.
Choose a method to test it: survey, interview, or observation. Write one reason for your choice.
Write four questions for your survey or interview.
Decide who you will ask, and how many people.

boxes.title: What makes a good survey question
lines: It is clear about what it is asking.
It relates to your topic and purpose.
It can be answered fairly quickly.
It is not leading. A leading question pushes people toward one answer, such as: Do you agree that our water is terrible?
Check each of your questions against that list. Rewrite any question that is unclear or leading. For example, change 'Do you agree the water is bad?' into 'How would you describe the water you use?'.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your prediction, your chosen method, and your four questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Are any of my questions leading or unclear? How would you fix them?
Ask the tutor whether my method really tests my prediction.

boxes.title: A real-world step
lines: With a trusted adult's help, ask your survey questions to a few family members or neighbours.
Bring what you find to your next teacher session and compare it with your prediction.

activities.title: Record and present your findings
activities.label: Activity 10: Record and present your findings
activities.intro: Findings are only useful if others can understand them. Once you have gathered information, decide the clearest way to record and present it. Your choice depends on the kind of information you have and on your audience.
steps: Write down your main findings so far, in short bullet points.
Decide the best form to present them: a table, a simple bar chart, a short written paragraph, or a few quotations from people you asked.
Write one sentence explaining why that form suits your information and your audience.
Make a first draft of your chosen form.

boxes.title: A model: Amal presenting her survey
lines: Finding: 12 of the 20 families she asked walk more than 20 minutes for water.
Best form: a simple bar chart, because the information is numbers and a chart shows the pattern at a glance.
Audience: her teacher and community, who can see the problem quickly from the chart.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what kind of information you gathered and who your audience is.
Ask it to suggest the clearest way to present your findings.
Ask the tutor to check whether my draft is clear and easy to understand.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'research' mean?
practice.answer: Research means finding out about something in an organised way, from more than one source, so you can trust it and explain it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: A good research question is clear, focused, and can be ______.
practice.answer: Argued (it can be argued).

practice.prompt: True or false: 'Why is plastic bad?' is a strong research question.
practice.answer: False. It is vague and it hides an opinion, so it is a weak question.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a primary source? (a) a textbook (b) a website (c) an interview you carry out (d) an encyclopaedia.
practice.answer: (c) an interview you carry out.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a secondary source? (a) a survey you run (b) a news article (c) watching a road yourself (d) interviewing a neighbour.
practice.answer: (b) a news article.

practice.prompt: Name two of the five parts that a reference should include.
practice.answer: Any two of: author, title, date published, where to find it (web address), date you looked at it.

practice.prompt: A question that pushes someone towards a particular answer is called a ______ question.
practice.answer: A leading question.

practice.prompt: To find the main idea of a paragraph, it helps to look for words that are ______.
practice.answer: Repeated.

practice.prompt: When you take notes, should you copy word for word, or use your own words?
practice.answer: Use your own words.

practice.prompt: A website address ending in ______ is usually an official government site.
practice.answer: .gov (an official government site).

practice.prompt: If a web address contains the word 'wiki', what should you remember?
practice.answer: Many people can edit wiki and social-media pages, so the information may not be correct; check it against a trusted source.

practice.prompt: You want to know how far many families walk for water. Which method fits best: survey, interview, or observation?
practice.answer: A survey (you want numbers from many people).

practice.prompt: Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own is called ______.
practice.answer: Plagiarism (copying).

practice.prompt: Put these search steps in order: (A) choose 3 to 6 keywords, (B) decide what information you need, (C) skim-read and save useful pages, (D) look past the first few results.
practice.answer: Correct order: B, A, D, C.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why referencing your sources is important.
practice.answer: Any one of: it is honest and avoids copying; it lets readers check your sources; it makes your work more trustworthy.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each research word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Primary source
options: A. A short version of a text, in your own words, keeping the key ideas.
B. First-hand information you gather yourself, such as a survey.
C. A note that says exactly where your information came from.
D. Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own.
E. Information made earlier by someone else, such as a book or website.
F. A smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.
practice.answer: B — First-hand information you gather yourself, such as a survey.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Secondary source
practice.answer: E — Information made earlier by someone else, such as a book or website.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Prediction
practice.answer: F — A smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Reference
practice.answer: C — A note that says exactly where your information came from.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Summary
practice.answer: A — A short version of a text, in your own words, keeping the key ideas.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Plagiarism
practice.answer: D — Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Leila wants to know what drivers actually do at a busy junction in Mogadishu. Which research method should she choose, and why?
practice.answer: Observation. Leila wants to know what drivers actually do, so watching and recording is the best method.

practice.prompt: Omar finds two websites about solar power. One ends in .org and names its authors; the other is an undated social-media post. Which should he trust more, and why?
practice.answer: The .org site with named authors is more trustworthy, because you can see who wrote it and organisations are usually more careful than an undated, unsigned post.

practice.prompt: Nadia reads a paragraph that keeps repeating the words 'sugar', 'drinks' and 'teeth'. What is she being told is the main idea?
practice.answer: The main idea is about how sugary drinks affect teeth. Repeated words point to the main idea.

practice.prompt: Idris found a great fact on a website but forgot to note where it came from. What problem will he have later, and what should he have done?
practice.answer: Idris cannot reference the fact, so he cannot prove where it came from and a reader could not check it. He should have noted the source straight away in his research journal.

practice.prompt: Amal wants to know how many families walk far for water, and also how they feel about it. Which two methods together would give her both the numbers and the feelings?
practice.answer: A survey to get the numbers from many families, and a few interviews to understand how they feel. Using two methods together gives a fuller answer.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour ...
Writing my ideas down in my research journal as I went ...

vocabulary.meaning: Finding out about something in an organised way, from more than one source.
The main question that guides your whole research project.
A smaller question that helps you answer your main research question.
Anywhere your information comes from: a person, book, website or video.
First-hand information you gather yourself, such as an interview or survey.
Information made earlier by someone else, such as a book or website.
Information on paper, such as a book, newspaper or printed report.
Information in digital form, such as a website, video, image or audio.
The way you gather information, such as a survey, interview or observation.
The same set of questions given to many people to find out what many think or do.
The written set of questions used in a survey.
A deeper conversation with one person or a small group to understand their views.
Carefully watching and recording what actually happens.
A smart guess about what you will find, which your research then tests.
A question that unfairly pushes someone toward one answer.
The most important point of a paragraph or a whole text.
Special words linked to a topic, such as borehole for a water topic.
Short reminders of the important ideas, written in your own words.
A short version of a text, in your own words, keeping only the key ideas.
Actually useful for answering your particular question.
A note saying exactly where a piece of information came from.
All your references gathered together at the end of your work.
Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are your own.
When a source unfairly leans to one side instead of being balanced.
Facts or information that support an idea or an answer.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
The point of view someone has, shaped by who they are and where they live.
An important word you type into a search engine to find information.
Able to be trusted; a reliable source is likely to be correct.
A notebook or file where you record your research as you go.

mistakes: Asking a question that is too broad, too narrow, or too vague.
Using only one source, or only sources that agree with you.
Trusting a website without checking who wrote it and when.
Copying words instead of writing notes in your own words.
Forgetting to note where a fact came from, so you cannot reference it later.
Writing a leading question that pushes people toward one answer.
Collecting lots of information but never organising or summarising it.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'research' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Research means finding out about something in an organised way, from more than one source, so you can trust it and explain it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: A good research question is clear, focused, and can be ______.
True or false: 'Why is plastic bad?' is a strong research question.
questions.modelAnswer: False. It is vague and it hides an opinion, so it is a weak question.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a primary source? (a) a textbook (b) a website (c) an interview you carry out (d) an encyclopaedia.
Which of these is a secondary source? (a) a survey you run (b) a news article (c) watching a road yourself (d) interviewing a neighbour.
Name two of the five parts that a reference should include.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: author, title, date published, where to find it (web address), date you looked at it.

questions.prompt: A question that pushes someone towards a particular answer is called a ______ question.
To find the main idea of a paragraph, it helps to look for words that are ______.
When you take notes, should you copy word for word, or use your own words?
A website address ending in ______ is usually an official government site.
If a web address contains the word 'wiki', what should you remember?
questions.modelAnswer: Many people can edit wiki and social-media pages, so the information may not be correct; check it against a trusted source.

questions.prompt: You want to know how far many families walk for water. Which method fits best: survey, interview, or observation?
questions.modelAnswer: A survey (you want numbers from many people).

selfAssessment.statement: I understand what the word 'research' means.
I can write research questions that are clear, focused and can be argued.
I can break a big question into helpful sub-questions.
I can tell the difference between primary and secondary sources.
I can choose a suitable research method to test a prediction.
I can judge whether a source can be trusted and is relevant.
I can take notes in my own words and find the main idea.
I can write a short summary in my own words.
I can reference a source with its author, title, date and location.
